newsitem.title: LEBANON: Japan asks to meet Lebanon detainees.
newsitem.headline: Japan asks to meet Lebanon detainees.

text.p: Japan asked Lebanese authorities on Tuesday to let its diplomats meet detainees reported held in Beirut on suspicion of belonging to the Japanese Red Army, Lebanese diplomatic sources said.

The request was conveyed by Japanese Ambassador Yasuji Ishikagi to Lebanese Foreign Minister Faris Bouez amid confusion after an unexplained series of apparently contradictory statements by Lebanese and Japanese officials over whether or not anybody was being held.

"The ambassador asked that Japanese diplomats meet those reported arrested by Lebanon and that the Lebanese government supply the Japanese government with all the information pertaining to the issue," one diplomatic source said.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo on February 18 that Lebanese authorities had told him they had arrested up to six Red Army members in the eastern Bekaa Valley.
But Lebanese Interior Minister Michel al-Murr and security sources have since denied that any Japanese are being held by Lebanese security agencies.
In Tokyo, the Japanese foreign ministry said on Tuesday it had no information on the case. "We have had no information from Lebanon on the case," a spokesman said.
Asked by reporters if he had received any confirmation about the identities of those reported arrested, Ishikagi replied: "No, no."

Speaking after meeting Bouez, he said: "I presented my government's request on this matter and I received from the foreign minister that when he gets more information on this matter he will duly let us know".

He added: "We are confident that the Lebanese authorities, security and judiciary and Lebanese government will handle this matter in the appropriate manner and we will know the results in due course."
Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon, controls the Bekaa valley where some of the guerrilla suspects were said to have been arrested.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. The Bekaa Valley was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war for guerrilla groups including Lebanese Moslems and Marxists, Palestinians, Kurds and the Japanese Red Army.
